final_proof:
Let
\[
I_1=\int_a^c f(t)\,dt,\qquad I_2=\int_c^b f(t)\,dt,
\qquad I=\int_a^b f(t)\,dt.
\]
Write \(f=u+iv\), where \(u=\operatorname{Re}f\) and \(v=\operatorname{Im}f\). Since \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), both \(u\) and \(v\) are continuous there and on the closed subintervals \([a,c]\) and \([c,b]\). Continuous real-valued functions on a closed bounded interval are Riemann integrable; hence all three complex integrals displayed above exist (with the complex integral defined by integrating real and imaginary parts).

If \(c=a\), then \(\int_a^c f=0\) and \(\int_c^b f=\int_a^b f\). If \(c=b\), the analogous statement holds. Thus it remains to consider \(a<c<b\).

We use the tagged-partition characterization of the Riemann integral: for every Riemann-integrable complex-valued function \(g\) on \([r,s]\) and every \(\eta>0\), there is \(\delta>0\) such that every tagged partition of \([r,s]\) of mesh less than \(\delta\), with Riemann sum \(S\), satisfies
\[
\left|S-\int_r^s g(t)\,dt\right|<\eta.
\]
(This follows componentwise from the corresponding real-valued characterization.)

Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Apply this characterization to \(f\) on each of \([a,c]\), \([c,b]\), and \([a,b]\), in every case with tolerance \(\varepsilon/3\). Let \(\delta>0\) be the minimum of the three resulting mesh bounds. Choose tagged partitions \(P_1\) of \([a,c]\) and \(P_2\) of \([c,b]\), each having mesh less than \(\delta\), and denote their Riemann sums by \(S_1\) and \(S_2\). Joining the partitions at their common endpoint \(c\), while retaining their tags, gives a tagged partition \(P\) of \([a,b]\) whose mesh is less than \(\delta\). Its Riemann sum \(S\) satisfies
\[
S=S_1+S_2,
\]
because its subintervals are precisely the subintervals belonging to \(P_1\) and \(P_2\).

The three choices of mesh bound now give
\[
|I_1-S_1|<\frac{\varepsilon}{3},\qquad
|I_2-S_2|<\frac{\varepsilon}{3},\qquad
|S-I|<\frac{\varepsilon}{3}.
\]
Since \(S=S_1+S_2\), the triangle inequality yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
|I_1+I_2-I|
&=|(I_1-S_1)+(I_2-S_2)+(S-I)|\\
&\le |I_1-S_1|+|I_2-S_2|+|S-I|\\
&<\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
\]
This holds for every \(\varepsilon>0\), so \(|I_1+I_2-I|=0\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \int_a^c f(t)\,dt+\int_c^b f(t)\,dt=\int_a^b f(t)\,dt}.
\]
